newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Nigeria reinforces in Sierra Leone, city calm.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria reinforces in Sierra Leone, city calm.

text.p: Regional power broker Nigeria airlifted more troops into Sierra Leone to bolster efforts to end a standoff with coup leaders and their rebel allies and to reinstate civilian President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.

Acting in the name of Sierra Leone's West African neighbours, Nigeria sent at least four helicopters packed with heavily armed soldiers to the capital where dissident soldiers and rebel forces forced it to give ground on Monday.

The United States carried out its largest single-day non-combatant evacuation from the city on Tuesday, bringing out 1,261 foreign and Sierra Leonian civilians by helicopter. The State Department said the airlift was likely to be the last.

General Victor Malu, field commander of the West African ECOMOG force, said Nigeria would bring in jet bombers and troop reinforcements to Freetown's Lungi international airport as part of efforts to overturn the May 25 coup by junior army officers.
"We agreed a ceasefire yesterday. We hope they will respect it because if not, we are building the capacity to carry on the offensive," Malu told Reuters on Tuesday.

Reports from the city, bombarded by Nigerians gunboats on Monday, described it as calm on Tuesday. Coup leaders put the death toll in the bombardment and subsequent fighting at 80. Hospital sources said at least 62 people had been killed.
Coup leader said they were holding 300 Nigerian soldiers who had surrendered as human shields against air attacks.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan told reporters at the Organisation of African Unity summit in Zimbabwe that efforts were continuing to resolve the stand-off peacefully.
"I hope one would be able to find a way of resolving this situation, for the coup makers to leave and for the legitimate government to go back without much bloodshed," he said.
Delegates to the summit said that African leaders resolved during a marathon closed session to isolate the rebel government and support West African efforts to restore democracy.
Sierra Leone's U.N. ambassador, James Jonah, said he had spoken to Kabbah, who was in neighbouring Guinea.
Jonah said ECOMOG was strengthening its positions before beginning a final assault on occupied government headquarters.
"When that is finished, they will go ahead with their objective, which is to remove these thugs who are parading as the government of Sierra Leone," he said.

Sierra Leone, a former British colony racked by civil war since 1991, has suffered three coups in five years. It is one of the world's poorest countries despite a wealth of gem-quality diamonds and other minerals.
The coup leaders have accused Kabbah of failing to consolidate a peace accord signed last November with rebel leader Foday Sankoh, and of encouraging ethnic conflict.
Sankoh, named as vice-chairman in Major Johnny Paul Koromah's ruling Armed Forces Revolutionary Council on Sunday, is being held in Nigeria.
He has told his men, who for the first time infiltrated Freetown in force after the latest coup, to back the coup.
Kabbah took office in 1996 after winning multi-party elections, which ended four years of military rule.
Britain said it was sending a naval support vessel with helicopters and a casualty receiving centre as a "prudent, precautionary measure". It will remain on standby offshore.
